Conversation and boundaries

How Do I Talk to My Partner About Their Drinking?

When to talk, which sentences work, what to expect afterwards - and what it feels like from the other side.

Steven H. White · approximately 9 min read

“The goal isn't to convince him. The goal is to say what's true.”

No single conversation solves the problem. But there is a difference between a conversation that builds a wall and one that opens a door, even just a crack.

You've probably rehearsed it a hundred times in your head. In the car, in the shower, at night when you couldn't sleep. You worked out what you'd say, and what he'd say back. And then either you didn't say it, or you did, and it went completely differently than you planned.

No single conversation solves the problem. That's important to know going in. But there is a difference between a conversation that builds a wall and one that opens a door, even just a crack.

From the inside: what did I hear when people talked to me?

I was the one people tried to talk to. And I was also the one who answered before the question was finished, who could turn any conversation around at any point. Outrage, attack, a raised voice: those were my tools.

When people tried to talk to me

I love my parents very much. But looking back, for many reasons, they couldn't communicate well. They swallowed things in silence, a great, great deal, and then they exploded. Not always at the worst incident, but when it had simply become too much for them. With a selfish addict who is struggling with his own personality and not seeing a lot of things clearly, that doesn't work. My response was usually irritation and outrage.

It's true that words often hit home, because I'm human, with a big ego. Shame and being found out bothered me too, just not the way they bothered them. They didn't handle those feelings well either. What reached me more was when I brushed up against the limits of my own “standards.”

Of course nobody can read minds, and that's hard. But there were, and are, moments when you can plant the seed of a thought. It takes a long time to sprout. But if the process is handled well, you can catch a meaningful moment when a person is more open.

Tone of voice always hit me especially hard.

Today I know it from the other side too. After eight or nine years of sobriety, my partner was the one drinking. Maybe I failed, like my parents did, despite all my experience and everything I'd learned. Or maybe she simply didn't care and didn't take me seriously. There are many reasons, but that's another story.

When not to bring it up

When he's been drinking. Someone who's been drinking can't think clearly. What you say won't stick, or it will turn into a fight.

When he's hungover. He's full of shame and irritability, and the smallest comment feels like an attack.

In the middle of an argument. If you're both already angry, the conversation will be about winning, not about drinking.

In front of others. Kids, relatives or friends turn it into a moment of shame, and shame builds walls.

And one more thing I learned the hard way: don't speak up only when you've had enough. If you swallow it for months and then everything bursts out at once, the other person doesn't hear your message. They hear the explosion.

When it's worth it

In a calm, sober moment, when there's time and nobody has to rush off. Just the two of you. Many people find that the day after a bad night, when the consequences are still fresh but the tension has eased, there's a better chance he'll actually listen.

How to say it

Talk about yourself, not about him. Sentences that start with “You always...” or “You never...” sound like accusations, and the answer to an accusation is defense. “I” sentences are harder to deflect, because they're about what you are going through.

Be specific, skip the labels. Say “You're an alcoholic” and denial is almost guaranteed. A specific thing that actually happened is much harder to deny: “Last night you couldn't remember what we talked about at dinner.”

Watch your tone. The same sentence means something completely different when it's sarcastic, shouted, or said in tired silence. Someone who is dependent is often more sensitive to tone than to content.

Keep it short. The longer the conversation, the more chances it has to drift. Say what you want to say, and don't expect to solve it on the spot.

Example sentences

These aren't magic words. They're there to show you how the same message sounds without blame.

Instead of: “You've been drinking again!”
Try: “I saw you drank a lot yesterday, and I'm worried.”

Instead of: “You're destroying this family!”
Try: “The kids were scared last night. I don't want them to get used to that.”

Instead of: “You're an alcoholic!”
Try: “I think drinking is taking up more and more space in our life.”

Instead of: “If you don't stop, I'm leaving!” - if you don't mean it.
Try: “I don't know how much longer I can live like this. I mean that.”

“I love you. That's exactly why I can't keep pretending I don't see it.”

“You don't have to answer now. I just want you to know how I feel.”

What to expect afterwards

Be prepared for the answer not to be the one you want. The most common reactions are denial, attack, changing the subject, or a promise that disappears a few days later.

That doesn't mean the conversation failed. For someone who is dependent, it matters that someone said it out loud, even if he rejects it in the moment. The sentence stays. A planted seed takes a long time to sprout, and you don't know when it will take effect.

The goal isn't to convince him

This may be the most important thing: the goal of the conversation isn't to convince him. The goal is to say what's true, so that you don't have to keep pretending you don't see anything.

And if it doesn't work, that's not your failure. I've sat on that side myself, with all my experience, and I didn't get through. Whether someone hears you is, in the end, not up to you.

If you want to set a boundary, set one you can keep yourself. Not about what he does, but about what you do. For example: “If you've been drinking, I won't get in the car with you.” That's your decision, and it's up to you to keep it.

There are also research-based programs designed specifically for family members that teach how to communicate in a way that protects you while increasing the chance that your partner seeks help. One example is the CRAFT approach. If you see a counselor, ask about it.

If the conversation becomes dangerous

If your partner becomes aggressive, makes threats, or you're afraid of him, stop the conversation and get to a safe place. If you're in danger, call your local emergency number: 112 in Europe, 999 in the UK, 911 in the US. No conversation is worth putting yourself in danger.

A few questions for yourself

What do I want him to know, even if he doesn't respond right now?

What boundary can I keep, regardless of what he does?

How long have I been swallowing this, and when do I usually explode?

Who can I talk to after the conversation if it gets hard?

Steven H. White - sober for ten years. Once he was the one people tried to talk to. Later, he was the one trying to talk to someone.

Say what is true

You cannot control whether your partner listens. You can choose your words, your timing, and a boundary you are able to keep.

One thing to remember

The goal is not to win the argument.

It is to say what you see, how it affects you, and what you will do to protect your boundary.
